profiles.meeting_scenario: The legal department of a legal-tech SaaS company is holding a design review of an existing approval package for a new document-isolation feature inspired by JFlow's information-flow model. The feature is intended for the company's hosted e-discovery platform, which processes privileged, personal, and export-controlled client documents. The package under review includes a draft internal legal memo, a customer-facing security whitepaper section describing the feature as using 'statically checked information flow,' and an open-source/provenance note about the engineering implementation. The agenda is to assess whether the package is legally sufficient, identify any gaps in representations or licensing analysis, and decide what revisions are needed before general counsel sign-off. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the current package is ready to move forward with only minor edits or whether additional documentation must be added.

members.name: Priya Malhotra
members.expertise: Technology transactions, SaaS product counseling, customer-facing product claims, and software licensing triage
members.background: Former big-law technology transactions associate who now supports product launches for a legal-tech vendor serving law firms and corporate legal departments.
members.private_state: She wants the approval package to clear this week so the launch does not slip into the next enterprise sales cycle, and she is trying to keep the review focused on the drafted artifacts rather than opening new workstreams.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the JFlow implementation,' they mean the company's in-house Java module that adopted the paper's ideas, not any historical academic prototype or sample code.
Describing the feature as 'statically checked' is accurate so long as static analysis is the primary enforcement mechanism, even if a few runtime label checks still exist at the edges.

The design review is about the legal sufficiency of the memo and customer-facing language, not the operational details of logging, retention, or SIEM routing unless those are already expressly claimed.
A package is 'ready for sign-off' once the legal risks are identified and the core wording is stable, even if appendices or supporting evidence are still being finalized.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.expertise: Security representations, privacy-by-design review, incident-response implications, and enterprise diligence readiness
members.background: Former regulator-side cyber counsel who joined the company to strengthen defensibility of security and privacy claims in customer and auditor reviews.
members.private_state: He wants a record that will withstand close customer diligence, and he is especially concerned about any overbroad technical statements or undocumented paths where sensitive labels or exception events could end up in logs.
hidden_assumptions: If engineering says they 'started from JFlow,' the legal provenance analysis should cover any Cornell-era code, annotations, or reference materials that may have been reused directly or indirectly.
A claim that the system is 'statically checked' will be read literally by sophisticated customers unless runtime enforcement is expressly carved out or qualified.
Reviewing exception behavior naturally includes where failed runtime label checks are logged, retained, and exposed operationally, because that can affect confidentiality representations.

A package is not 'ready for sign-off' until the supporting appendix is complete enough that procurement, security reviewers, or auditors could rely on it without coming back for missing substantiation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the whitepaper can say the feature uses 'statically checked information flow.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes 'statically checked' to mean the architecture relies predominantly on compile-time checking, with limited runtime checks still comfortably inside that description.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes 'statically checked' to mean customers will infer enforcement is entirely or effectively complete at compile time, so any meaningful runtime label checking needs qualification.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the technical literature and sounds precise, so both assume they are preserving the same core claim even though one treats it as an umbrella description and the other as a near-literal representation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the implementation' or 'the JFlow code' during the provenance discussion.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking only of the current internal repository written by the company's engineers and reviewed under ordinary internal IP clearance procedures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader implementation lineage, including any academic prototype code, sample annotations, or reference artifacts engineers may have drawn from when building the feature.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In product-counsel conversations, 'the implementation' usually refers to the present codebase, while in diligence-oriented security and provenance review it often includes antecedent materials; both uses are normal enough that neither speaker hears the ambiguity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'the exception path' should be covered in the package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the memo should address whether exception semantics undermine the customer-facing claim that privileged data will not flow to lower-clearance outputs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this also includes operational consequences of runtime label-check failures, such as whether exception payloads or labels are logged to monitoring systems and retained under standard log policies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Exception handling sounds like a single technical topic, and both are used to discussing it as a risk bucket; the boundary between semantic correctness and operational logging is easy to leave implicit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both repeatedly ask whether the package is 'ready for sign-off.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the draft is mature enough for legal approval in principle, with minor cleanup and supporting attachments allowed to follow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the package is complete enough that external-facing diligence questions could be answered immediately from the approved record.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In internal legal meetings, 'sign-off' often functions as a shorthand milestone rather than a defined approval threshold, so both can sincerely say yes while applying different completion standards.
